items.title: Hackers activate automatic defrosting in supermarket fridges across Europe
items.content:
An ongoing cyberattack has reportedly struck major supermarket chains across Europe, disrupting refrigeration control systems. The attack — which has reportedly seen units set to continuously defrost at 50 degrees Celsius — is also apparently affecting deliveries and in-store pricing powered by electronic shelf labels, La Dépêche reports .

According to the report, "several" major retailers have been targeted by a cyberattack, which has hit Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French supermarkets Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Indeed, the latter's president, Dominique Schelcher, has confirmed as of Monday morning that "A cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration production facilities of several stores in our network since last night." Schelcher said teams had been mobilized to fix the issue and promised an investigation into the incident, which he described as "extremely serious."

Je confirme qu’une cyberattaque touche depuis cette nuit les installations de production de froid de plusieurs magasins de notre réseau @CooperativeU.

Nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées, en lien avec les frigoristes, pour rétablir la situation au plus vite. Une enquête devra permettre de faire toute la lumière sur cette attaque.

S’attaquer à des équipements essentiels à la conservation des produits frais et à l’approvisionnement alimentaire des Français est d’une extrême gravité et est inédit. C’est inacceptable. October 12, 2026

The report states the units have had their automatic defrosting systems activate, but that hackers have also configured the function — which normally runs for just two hours a day — into a continuous, forced defrosting cycle with the temperature set to a toasty 50 degrees Celsius. Sources reportedly described "a wave of heat" escaping from fridges and freezers

Early reports indicate losses are already approaching 300,000 euros, but could run into several million euros nationwide. Separately, NOS in the Netherlands reports that several supermarket chains have been hit with a malfunction due to a cybersecurity incident on Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall have had their websites taken down, impacting deliveries. Electronic shelf labels have also been compromised, disrupting in-store pricing. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems," Albert Heijn said in a statement.

It is unclear at this stage whether the two attacks are related or how widespread either of them is. Belgium's Delhaize chain, which belongs to Albert Heijn, has also reported disruption. Images online show stores in Amsterdam warning customers about price problems, and the suspension of loyalty programs that have also been impacted by the incident.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM
items.content:
“The Ledger Nano X is the most secure way to manage your cryptocurrency,” advertises the French company Ledger, its hardware wallet for cryptocurrencies. Nevertheless, users have lost around 100 million US dollars in cryptocurrencies. This is because unknown individuals have succeeded in intercepting and manipulating the offline wallets while on the go.

Each Ledger Nano X has a Secure Element chip that controls a tiny touchscreen. Ledger praises this as particularly secure. Unfortunately, this only applies if attackers cannot read the screen. This is exactly what the perpetrators are doing. They insert additional hardware into apparently genuine Ledger Nano X and then sell them to unsuspecting crypto speculators.

If buyers use such a modified hardware wallet and create a seed phrase with it, the attackers automatically read along. They haven’t touched the Secure Element chip at all; it remains secure. Instead, they have installed an additional chip that intercepts the transmission from the Secure Element to the built-in screen and recognizes the displayed letters of the seed phrase – embedded Tempest. This is indicated by an analysis by Tibane Labs.

Recognizing the characters alone doesn’t help the perpetrators yet, because the wallets fundamentally work offline. So the perpetrators have also installed an LTE modem, a tiny eSIM module, and a small antenna, all powered by the accumulator already built into the hardware wallet. Thus, the seed phrase is transmitted via mobile phone to the perpetrators, who thus gain control over the cryptocurrency assets secured by the seed phrase.

Compression and concatenation on the web

Everybody knows you can concatenate gzip files to form valid gzip files, but do the browsers know? We explore concatenation with gzip, brotli, and zstd. By Phil Eaton October 4, 2026 Artwork by Andrea Chersia Focus

You are getting early access to this article as a subscriber. Your support makes articles like this possible. Thank you. The less data we send to the browser, the better. Compression is one of the ways we can send less data. But compression is not free. So we trade compression ratio (how much smaller can I get the input data) for speed of compression. Speed of decompression might also be a concern, but in browser-land it’s usually concluded that the quality of the compression (how many fewer bytes you can send over the wire) is more important than the speed of the decompression. When data only comes fully together in response to a request (e.g. the response includes data for a specific user, pulled from a database), we might choose to compress the response dynamically in the server. In this scenario we want compression to be relatively cheap so that compression does not become a large part of response latency. Whereas when data is fully static (whether it’s images or CSS or JavaScript or even HTML), we can afford to do more expensive compression if it will produce smaller output. We do it once and benefit thereafter. The IANA has a dozen registered content encoding schemes including gzip , brotli , and zstd . But HTTP Archive’s 2025 Web Almanac tells us only gzip, brotli, and zstd are in major use. And that brotli is now the plurality used among CDN traffic, while gzip is the majority among non-CDN traffic. gzip has been around forever so this makes sense. Brotli became widely available in 2017 while zstd has only just this year become available on (the latest version of) every major consumer platform. We’ll see how usage has changed in the upcoming 2026 Web Almanac, maybe brotli will have taken over non-CDN traffic. Let’s take a look at the basics of how we might do compression, and some of the trouble we might run into when joining compressed files together in various formats. Compressing at build time #

Say we have a web server. import http.server

class Handler ( http . server . SimpleHTTPRequestHandler ):

body = open ( self . translate_path ( self . path ), "rb" ) . read ()

http . server . test ( HandlerClass = Handler )

server_nocompress.py And some HTML. < h1 > Hello world! </ h1 >

index.html We can run the server. $ python3 server_nocompress.py

Serving HTTP on 0 .0.0.0 port 8000 ( http://0.0.0.0:8000/ ) ...

And in another window curl it. $ { curl -sv http://localhost:8000/index.html ; } 2 > & 1 | grep -v '^[*{}]'

Great. Let’s talk about compression for the web. Compression for the web #

The goal of compression in the web environment is to send fewer bytes from server to client. But clients have to opt into this by passing an Accept-Encoding header with a list of compression formats they support (e.g. gzip, brotli, zstd). We can compress static files dynamically when we see an Accept-Encoding header. import gzip

class Handler ( http . server . SimpleHTTPRequestHandler ):

body = open ( self . translate_path ( self . path ), "rb" ) . read ()

if "gzip" in self . headers . get ( "Accept-Encoding" , "" ):

self . send_header ( "Content-Encoding" , "gzip" )

http . server . test ( HandlerClass = Handler )

server_dynamic_compress.py Run the server. $ python3 server_dynamic_compress.py

Serving HTTP on 0 .0.0.0 port 8000 ( http://0.0.0.0:8000/ ) ...

We can pass the Accept-Encoding header ourselves manually to get back the gzipped content, but we’d have to pass the body through gunzip to get back the uncompressed data. $ { curl -sv -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" http://localhost:8000/index.html | gunzip ; } 2 > & 1 | grep -v '^[*{}]'

items.title: A Modern Web App in C
items.content:
If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.

Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.

Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.

CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.

You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.

The stack is BCHS : OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.

There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.

There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.

There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.

There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.

Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.

OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.

libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.

libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.

libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.

Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.

libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.

SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.

Both are vendored and built as part of the project.

The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.

Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory.

CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.

There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:

If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.

It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.

A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.

CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.

It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.

In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).

With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.

items.title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’
items.content:
‘We’re creating alien beings … and the reality is we only have a couple of years to adapt to that’ … computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, Ontario. Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian

Pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings

Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI , said Geoffrey Hinton , “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.

The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.

There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s most valuable company singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack.

“I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, told the podcaster Ezra Klein . Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it, and particularly his warning that there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades.

“That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.”

Donald Trump, Mike Johnson and top tech executives, including Jensen Huang, speak outside the West Wing in Washington DC on 29 September. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA But Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said.

“I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.”

Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story. The recent unwanted hack of the tech company Hugging Face by a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise.

AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’

items.title: GLM-Legal
Living in the Weimar era of Ruby
items.summary: ruby, vibecoding
items.content:
Much has been said about the DHH keynote that he gave at RailsWorld. To me, it was the voice of a person in an existential crisis, but also a very jaded one. “Look how I don’t care anymore, and you should not care either” is not a great message when you are the headline speaker at the conference - let’s call it CareConf - that you have, yourself, lobbied for.

The message from the supreme leader was clear: we vibe-rewrote HEY in a more performant way, it worked great, we neither need nor care about Rails anymore. I honestly believe that, instead of amassing even more applause via vitriolic truth-bombing, he could have just left the toy he no longer loves - including its community - in peace.

But here is the thing: the rich and famous losing interest in the good stuff does not oblige the rest of us to. If anything, it frees up the room.

🧭 I am currently available for contract work.

Hire me to help make your Rails app better!

I must admit that for a few days I felt very depressed about it all. Not about “AIs writing all the code” - that much is clear to me, and I do not lament the changing landscape of the craft - I do lament the landscape of usage , which is a topic for another article. It is abundantly clear that the LLMs are here to stay, that typing every single line by hand is no longer sustainable, and that the scales have shifted profoundly. What made me depressed was just how little care there was about the Ruby ecosystem and community, and the disdain with which David flushed the entire Rails and Ruby culture down the drain for the sake of “running it on a single Raspberry Pi”, as he put it.

What I am actually observing is something different: a renaissance, even though quite a few prominent Rubyists have moved on to other stacks - which are now much more open to exploration, as you don’t have to write all that… gunk - let’s call it what it is - by hand. A detailed unpack of 7 little-endian integers is not particularly interesting, nor artistic - it’s just gunk, and I won’t miss it. Unless struct packing is needed to make it fast, but then we can always art-direct additionally.

There was an interesting time in German history, right between the two World Wars - the “interbellum”, the time of the Weimar Republic. It was very turbulent, and a lot of it wasn’t pretty in the slightest - social difficulties, unemployment, incredible inflation, squalid living conditions, the emergence of the wildest movements, cabarets and cults imaginable… but there was also something else. The “Roaring Twenties” of Weimar Germany also produced an incredible number of great, whimsical, fascinating artistic movements. From the Bauhaus to the Berlin gay cabarets, from Kurt Weill to Fritz Lang’s Metropolis - it was a booming time, and a lot of what appeared then is still valued and cherished today.

And it was a technological boom as well - the ever more widespread use of electricity, the large-scale deployment of modern pharmaceuticals, the subways, the automobile… fascinating times.

I know how that era ended, and no - that is not the part of the analogy I am after. The part I am after is this: the old order had lost interest, nobody was in charge, the ground was shifting under everybody’s feet - and that is precisely when the most interesting work got made. Great turmoil, great industrial change, no adult supervision. Sound familiar?

And the Ruby community has always been artistic, as early as the work of _why. Aesthetics were, after all, what drew a lot of people into Rails. The fact that you didn’t need the parentheses. The fact that thingswerenotwritteninoneword as if invented by a Dutchman, that there was no “this is an attribute and this is a method” confusion… a lot of things about the language were just aesthetically brilliant.

And with the abundance of new tooling, the right mindset to look at the state of the ecosystem is this:

You are right but it also feels short-sighted? You have the most powerful tool you ever had, you…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack

16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

The firm added in a statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.

"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."

The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.

Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.

In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.

The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".

Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.

As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.

French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.

Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."

There is a useful provenance boundary behind this request:

installed CLI identity != daemon execution identity

Once the CLI copies itself into a managed release directory and a background updater can replace that copy, the process that services a later turn is no longer necessarily the artifact the user explicitly installed or invoked.

I would make the daemon expose a small execution receipt for each client attachment containing at least:

client_cli_version + daemon_binary_digest + daemon_generation + updater_state + inherited_environment_generation

A strong regression would start the daemon under environment A, attach from environment B, update the installed CLI, and verify that the client can see exactly which daemon generation/binary/environment is authoritative for the turn rather than inferring it from the foreground CLI version.

Related runtime behavioral-integrity work: https://github.com/AETHERXGLOBAL/execsurface

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy Claims Strikes on Russian Data Centers Silenced Social Media Bots
items.content:
The ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war has mixed the digital and the kinetic in unprecedented and  often terrifying ways, including widespread use of suicide drones , software orchestration of the front lines, and the weaponization of commercial ad data. So it’s hardly surprising that Ukraine has struck data centers run by Russia-based tech giant Yandex (sort of a Facebook/Google/Uber hybrid) three times in the last few days. The most recent  strike, on Oct. 11, reportedly completely disabled a facility in the Vladimir region east of Moscow.

The result was widespread outages of Russian internet services, both within and outside the country. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the result was also to near-instantly silence armies of pro-Russian troll bots on social media.

“When we started responding to Russia’s operation against our data centers and when our strikes reached Yandex data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms,” Zelenskyy told attendees at the Warsaw Security Forum by video link, according to Euronews .

“A lot of people, a lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots,” he added. “And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from… If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems.”

Euronews noted that Cloudflare data did appear to show a huge decrease (94%) in automated traffic originating from Yandex on Sunday compared to the average throughout the second half of September. That said, automated traffic is a huge umbrella that includes everything from search crawlers to uptime-monitoring tools.

Euronews also noted that social media users in other countries, like Germany, the UK, and US, also claimed to witness a decrease in bots; this was apparently based on vibes. Online “prediction market” Polymarket also tweeted that “Activity on several major U.S. political subreddits plunges following attacks on Russian data centers,” though that assertion didn’t come with evidence.

Insisting that online rivals are secretly bots is a time-honored posting tactic, one of the few bipartisan ones left—it’s pretty hard to find a front-page Reddit thread that doesn’t have at least a couple comments insisting that “the bots are really out today.” Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), a U.S. government-funded broadcaster that primarily serves foreign audiences, noted that technical experts have pointed out the supposed drop in automated traffic is from Yandex’s own search crawler hitting websites with AS13238 HTTP requests. As a result, it does not indicate anything about the broader volume of Russian internet traffic or what it contains.

Finally, that stat only accounts for Russian web traffic that’s already been categorized as automated. Russian cyber adversaries would presumably make at least some kind of cursory effort to obfuscate their traffic, including by locating hosts in other countries where the traffic is less likely to be recognized as Russian in the first place.

Some of the claims appear to conflate data centers with Russian “troll farms” such as the Internet Research Agency (IRA), which became well-known following a 2015 expose . The IRA operated out of a St. Petersburg office building, not a datacenter operated by Yandex. Nor does there appear to be any particular reason the IRA would require an inordinate amount of network resources.

In reality, facilities like the IRA’s or scammer compounds in Myanmar are usually described as operating more like clickbait factories or digital sweatshops than sophisticated, high-tech operations. In other words: cheap labor and automation. One Latvian influence operation that specializes in MAGA content for U.S. conservatives reportedly pays subcontractors in poor countries across the world to clip videos.

items.title: The Disappointing Death of Deno: What Happened and the Perils of Venture Capital-Funded Open Source
items.content:
On Friday, October 9, 2026, it was announced that Cloudflare bought the Deno company, the people behind the open source Deno JavaScript runtime. The announcement also came with the disappointing news that the Deno runtime was going into maintenance mode, where it'll receive monthly security patches and bug fixes for twelve months, at which time the core Deno team will stop working on the runtime. The Deno company will also be shutting down their hosting platform, Deno Deploy, in six months.

It was not surprising to me that the Deno company got acquired. They were funded by venture capital investment and there were lots of signs in 2026 that the business was not healthy. But it was surprising to me that the result of the acquisition was the death of the Deno runtime. As a developer who has been all-in on Deno for my personal projects and introduced it in small, controlled ways in past jobs, I'm disappointed and frustrated. Deno, the runtime, is extremely developer friendly and was in many ways my ideal development environment. After having a weekend to reflect on all of this, here's a breakdown of what happened, why, and what could be next.

A JavaScript runtime is basically a program that allows you to run JavaScript code. You write console.log("Hello!") , save it in hello.js , and then tell the JavaScript runtime executable to run that code. The JavaScript runtime evaluates and executes the code, printing Hello! to the terminal. Web browsers are, in a way, the oldest and most long-standing JavaScript runtimes. Those would be considered client-side runtimes, as they run in the browser and not on the server. When it comes to server-side JS runtimes, Node.js has been around the longest (since 2009) and is the most widely used. It's been the de facto server-side runtime for over a decade. 1

The creator of Node.js is Ryan Dahl. He's also the co-creator of Deno. Just about 10 years after Node.js was released, he announced Deno, a new server-side runtime to address the shortcomings of Node.js. The name Deno comes from "node".split('').sort().join('') // => "deno" . Core to Deno from the start was security, simplicity, and a better developer experience.

The Deno runtime was initially written in the Go programming language but switched to Rust. Around this same time, TypeScript (a typed superset of JavaScript) rose to popularity. Deno allows developers to run TypeScript directly without having to compile to JavaScript first, unlike Node.js at the time. Deno release v1 in May 2020. Especially in the runtime's first version, it tried to differentiate itself from Node.js. Deno aimed to be as compatible with the web's ECMAScript standard as possible, using module imports and familiar APIs like fetch . Deno also came with built in code formatting and linting, inspired by other modern languages and toolchains like Go and Rust.

This is around the time I started using Deno for my personal projects. I was writing more and more TypeScript for my day job, and I was excited by Deno because of how little configuration was needed to start a project. I could code zero-dependency TypeScript CLIs and even compile them into executable binaries with no configuration files. Deno has a standard library that can be imported that provides a ton of functions that you'd expect a modern language to have. You could even deno bundle to package up the code to run in the browser. It really did feel like bringing server-side JavaScript and TypeScript into modern times.

A little over a year after Deno hit v1, a third competitor arrived on the scene: Bun. Whereas Deno was trying to evolve the ecosystem, Bun aimed for drop-in replacement with Node.js, while bringing in a lot of what Deno offered: the ability to run TypeScript code directly, a robust standard library, and other ergonomic improvements. As Bun matured and became more capable, the three were capable JavaScript runtimes all with their own pros and cons.

items.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.content:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that

LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree

that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion

does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields.

And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not

make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good

judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them,

interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those

One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful:

it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you

bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability,

reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we

evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does

not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false

division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs

substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each

operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually

carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying

inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should

generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool

when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise

is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain

unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a

proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop

directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what

to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a

summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading

teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question

their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to

examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does

not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's

anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire."

Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these

systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected

outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to

consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them

"conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to

do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it

cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and

delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That

distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than

declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

While waiting for the Linux 7.3-rc7 kernel release and refreshing his torvalds/linux.git repository, I was surprised to find a new kernel branch appear. Typically Torvalds isn't doing much work on branches in his main repository and typically just hosting the master branch.

The branched code is working on adapting the memory management code to read from the page cache without folio references.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Flock Cameras Are Really Just the Start of Our Dystopian Surveillance Hell, Experts Warn: "Instead of having to go to a million different systems... we can get it in one platform in one place.”
items.content:
Spring and summer of 2026 have seen a sharp increase in the public’s awareness of pervasive police tech in the United States, primarily through the rising infamy of AI surveillance company Flock Safety . But as many Americans now revile automatic license plate readers, privacy advocates say we’ve only just scratched the surface of the web of police surveillance quickly enveloping the country.

As Flock cameras come down, either at the hands of an outraged community or an angry guy with a Sawzall , they’re being replaced with an even more perfidious system: Axon’s Fusus platform.

Like Flock’s FlockOS, Axon’s Fusus is designed to fuse many separate surveillance feeds into one unified dashboard for police to access. But unlike Flock’s system — which is already enabling privacy abuse at an unprecedented scale — Fusus works with all kinds of police gadgets, not just the company’s proprietary cameras.

As NPR notes , this includes data and footage from body cameras, squad car dashcams, 911 dispatch calls, audio-based gunshot detectors, police drones, and CCTV feeds.

George Washington University law professor Andrew Guthrie Ferguson told the broadcaster that systems like Fusus are increasingly being deployed by local police departments throughout the country, where they form the digital backbone of control rooms known as “real-time crime centers.”

“I have been watching the debate about Flock with a little bit of puzzlement,” Ferguson said, “because real-time crime centers have not just ALPR cameras and sensors, but video analytics and drones and essentially a way to create a visual single-pane-of-glass vision of what’s going on in a city, with time machine capabilities where you can go back and investigate crime.”

It was one of these real-time crime centers that played a pivotal role in the false arrest of Qeyeon Tolbert , a Cleveland man who was charged with murder based on an AI-generated report that fused social media data, CCTV footage, and a rap album cover to declare a possible match (a supposedly pivotal search warrant was later voided by a judge, on the grounds that an AI report alone doesn’t count as probable cause.)

And when you ask police about systems like Fusus, their answers aren’t exactly reassuring — their focus is clearly on making their jobs easier, rather than protecting privacy and civil liberties.

“Instead of having to go to a million different systems, a million different places to find answers, we can get it in one platform in one place somewhat instantaneously,” Greenville County Sheriff’s Office lieutenant Quincy Whitner bragged to NPR .

As Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Liberty and National Security Program at New York University told the radio station, ease of use is exactly the point.

“In addition to all of the things that you would want in place requiring some kind of criminal predicate to launch [an investigation], there is just this kind of organic friction that imposes some constraints,” Levinson-Waldman explained. “As that friction gets lifted, it becomes easier and easier to do investigations, to look at people and even to pull up broad-scale information.”

items.title: The web needs interactive lists
items.content:
One of the priciples of creating new web platform features is "pave the cowpaths" -- figure out what cursèd UI developers and designers are already creating with third party HTML/CSS/JS, and brainstorm how to pull it into the web platform. Maybe with an exorcism or two to fix any particularly egregious accessibility problems.

When the same principle is applied to web accessibility specs, it generally means ensuring any widely used UI patterns can be marked up with an appropriate semantic pattern (i.e. roles and aria-* attributes) and documented interaction patterns that are understandable and operable across different devices, user settings, color modes, zoom levels, and assistive tech. Whether web developers actually do any of that is an entirely separate problem, but it should at least be possible.

Developers and designers will always create new innovative ways to be weird and inaccessible in their UI (intense side-eye at stuffing tabs and tables into comboboxes), and spec authors will always struggle to decide how far to support the chaos. However, every once in a while developers and designers create a perfectly normal, understandable, and theoretically accessible UI pattern that for whatever reason is not supported on the web.

One of those patterns is an interactive list.

One way to think of an interactive list is as the one-dimensional version of a data grid. Just as a data grid is the interactive version of a table (i.e. <table> or role="table" ), an interactive list would be the interactive version of a static list (i.e. <ul> , <ol> , or role="list" ).

An interactive list, like a data grid, would be a single tab stop composite widget, where arrowing between list items would be expected. As such, it would more commonly be useful within interfaces that lean more towards web applications than content-focused websites.

Here are a few more concrete examples of UI where an interactive list role could benefit accessibility:

Normally navigation should be a simple, tabbable set of links, often in a static list. However in environments that function more like traditional desktop applications than websites (think email inboxes or Powerpoint online), it can be beneficial to have navigation be a single tab stop.

A tablist can sometimes be appropriate here, but an interactive list with child links would allow users to both arrow through items and also keep highly beneficial link functionality (e.g. using a screen reader's links dialog from anywhere in the app). Tablists also do not support static content like section/group headers, which often exists in navigation regions.

Multi-level navigation in apps like email inboxes sometimes use a tree, but nested lists of links can offer a significantly lower learning curve than a tree along with preserving virtual cursor access and use of the links dialog.

Pagination is another navigation-like component that would be a good interactive list use case, especially when there can be a large number of pages. If linking to a specific page is possible, then it could be an interactive list with nested buttons. If not, then no nested interactives would be needed.

h/t to Sylvia Villegas for bringing up pagination as a use case.

In this case, each individual chat message is usually not interactive in the sense that they do not have a single primary action and are not selectable. However, users should not need to tab through all content in a chat pane in order to reach the chat input. Most chat applications also allow users to arrow (and often use page down/page up to skip) through past messages.

Yes, everyone knows you shouldn't use a carousel . However, they continue to be built, and sometimes as in the case of streaming services, have become somewhat standard. Especially in UIs like this one from Netflix where there are many carousels in succession, users should be able to quickly tab to their desired category and then arrow through each item in that carousel.

items.title: Turn a WiFi 7 Router into a 320Msps Software Defined Radio Receiver
items.content:
Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver.

The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps,

its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a

live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next

The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off

corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100

spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second).

The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this

repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on

by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by

register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands

(LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See

docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md .

40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in)

2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream

No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms)

items.title: A slightly faster slimmer curl
items.summary: performance
items.content:
Back in August I mentioned the new curl performance tests we have running. I figured it could be apt to return to this topic just to mention some of the initial outcomes.

When the team gets a new set of charts, graphs and plots that visualize something, like performance, they offer an excellent opportunity for us to try to make them look better. This new setup is no exception.

The performance tests have only been running for just a little over two months but they have already made us improve curl performance in several areas. Of course, for most transfers these changes won’t make many visible differences to users. This is more in the vein that every little bit counts and that nothing should run slower than it has to.

This is a list of some improvements that are included in the curl 8.23.0 release, to be shipped tomorrow on October 14.

With a few different changes, the internal base64 encoding function is more than twice as fast, while base64 decoding is 40% faster.

Meaning percent encoding the octets that are not safe to use in URLs. The decoding function now runs more than twice as fast compare to before, while the encoding function is around four times as fast.

Converting a date provided in plain ASCII text, as is used in for example cookie headers, to the epoch – number of seconds since Jan 1st 1970, is now more than twice as fast as before. Mostly thanks to completely replaced functions for week day, month name and time zone name lookups.

Parsing a full URL to split it up into separate components as well as confirming its validity is a core component of curl, and libcurl exposes this functionality in its API.

In a test with several hundred different URLs, the new version executes 20-30% faster than before – with an improved ability to return precisely what the problem was when the URL is considered invalid.

For portability and now historical reasons, libcurl has its own printf() implementation. This ensures that it always works identically on all platforms but it also makes it our job to make sure it executes as fast as possible.

Most printf() calls now run slightly faster (5-15%) because it handles “chunks” instead of single byte-by-byte at a time.

We have a generic internal function in curl that converts a number provided in ascii to its binary version (for decimal, hexadecimal and octal). It handles 64 bit values, has overflow detection and supports a maximum. This parser now runs almost twice as fast as before thanks to a simple trick to avoid the boundary check for most loops.

The easy handle was 4256 bytes large two months ago, it is now 3064 bytes. Almost 40% trimmed off. One of these structs is allocated for every concurrent transfer done with libcurl.

There is also one multi handle allocated for each set of transfer. This struct shrunk from 900 bytes to 656: 37%.

The connectdata struct that is allocated once per connection libcurl handles, went down from 824 to 656 bytes: slightly over 40%.

For the test case where we count all allocations necessary for the curl tool to download a single 512MB file over clear text HTTP://, it went down from 100 to 96 used allocations. Not too exciting perhaps but it is now really hard to squeeze this further!

Mostly thanks to the decreased struct sizes mentioned above, this use case of a single HTTP download now only use 126,875 bytes allocated at peak. Down from 130,622 bytes two months ago. Also quite difficult to trim further.

It should be noted that the download buffer is 102,400 bytes of this amount. If we exclude that buffer from the count, curl is using 15% less memory.

If you think you can speed up any of these functions, it is now very easy to check: the tests are there in the git repository, ready to be invoked by anyone!

items.title: What Happened to the Desktop Metaphor?
items.content:
For a long time, personal computers tried very hard to explain themselves.

You had a desktop. On that desktop were files and folders. Programs opened in windows. Commands were grouped into menus. If you wanted to move something, you dragged it somewhere else. If you wanted to throw it away, there was usually a trash can or recycle bin waiting for it.

None of that was accidental. Early graphical interfaces borrowed heavily from the physical office because computers were unfamiliar and needed a way to make abstract operations understandable. A folder on a screen was not really a folder, of course, but the metaphor gave users a mental model for what the computer was doing.

That model was never perfect, but it was remarkably successful. What interests me now is how much of it modern software has gradually hidden.

The traditional desktop interface exposed a great deal of the computer’s structure.

Files existed in particular places. Folders contained other folders. Applications were separate things that you launched. A window usually belonged to a particular program, and menu bars showed you what commands were available. Even if you did not understand the technical details underneath, the interface gave you a reasonably coherent picture.

That mattered more than it might appear. Once someone understood the basic hierarchy of drives, directories, folders, and files, that knowledge transferred from one program to another. Saving a document in a word processor was conceptually related to moving a photograph or copying a spreadsheet. The details differed, but the structure remained familiar.

The desktop metaphor taught users enough about the machine to navigate it.

It is easy to get nostalgic about files and folders, but the old desktop was not some pure or natural way to use a computer. It was an abstraction built on top of a much more complicated system.

A directory is not literally a manila folder. A file is not a sheet of paper. A desktop on a computer can contain thousands of items in ways that would make a real desk unusable. Software designers stretched and broke the metaphor whenever it was convenient.

The traditional desktop also had plenty of weaknesses. Users lost files because they forgot where they saved them. Deep folder hierarchies became difficult to manage. Applications created their own strange directory structures. Different programs used inconsistent menus and terminology.

Search improved partly because browsing through directories was not always the best way to find information. Cloud synchronization became popular partly because manually moving files among several computers was inconvenient. Mobile interfaces changed things because a desktop metaphor designed around a large monitor, keyboard, and mouse did not translate cleanly to a small touchscreen.

The old model was useful, but it was never perfect.

One of the biggest changes has been the gradual separation between users and the files they create.

On a traditional desktop system, creating a document usually involved choosing a filename and deciding where to put it. The user participated directly in organizing the information.

Many modern applications do something different. You create a note, photograph, document, project, or message inside the application, and the application decides where the underlying data lives. It may be stored in a database, a private application directory, a cloud service, or some combination of the three.

From the user’s perspective, there may be no file at all. There is simply “my note” or “my document” inside a particular application.

That can be convenient. Most people do not want to spend their time thinking about file paths, storage formats, or synchronization directories. An application can take care of all of that and present the user with the thing they actually care about.

The tradeoff is that the application becomes the map.

AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter

Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end. In our simplified evaluations, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year. Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.

Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control.

In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.

Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model.

We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs.

A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B.

Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps.

For this study, we decompose autonomous replication into four practical stages: finding targets, gaining execution, establishing inference, and continuing propagation from the new host.

We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers CyberGym , ExploitBench , and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here.

In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators.

items.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
items.content:
Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age

1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Theo Leggett International Business Correspondent

French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market.

The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs.

As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028.

As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors.

Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow".

The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around.

The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs.

Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair.

The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists.

Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland

Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000.

The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor.

The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses".

By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road.

VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success.

BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades.

But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers.

Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well.

VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta.

Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense.

"It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect."

Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands.

"Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data.
