items.title: (Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers
items.summary: cryptography
items.content:
(Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers

Publishing “Cryptographic Right Answers” for developers is a tradition by now. Colin Percival started in 2009 , Thomas Ptacek followed up in 2015 , and then Latacora carried on in 2018 and 2024 .

It might feel too soon for an update, but so much has changed . The timeline of the post-quantum transition dramatically shifted in early 2026 , and there is now consensus that it needs to complete by 2029. 2029! We have three years!

The good news is that, despite what you might have heard, symmetric cryptography is going to be fine, because Grover does not matter . The bad news is that all asymmetric answers changed compared to 2018 and most even compared to 2024.

The answers below assume you are not constrained by any specific compliance regime, although they are mostly compatible with FIPS 140. 1 If you need to follow something stricter like CNSA 2.0, you’ll know. Just substitute as appropriate.

Finally, remember the other big change of 2026: LLMs are very good at finding bugs now. “Get a review from the best model you can afford” is now firmly a Cryptographic Right Answer, along with the long-time classic “use a memory-safe language.”

If you’re in a rush, here’s the cheat sheet:

Encrypting data : If you’re in the cloud, KMS. Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128.

Symmetric key length : Don’t stress it. 256-bit keys if you need to pick.

Hash algorithm : SHA-2 is still fine, but use a real multihash (SequenceHash) if needed.

Random IDs : 32 random bytes, a.k.a. 256-bit random numbers.

Password handling : Argon2id or scrypt. But have you considered passkeys instead?

Key exchange : X25519+ML-KEM-768 in a secure, standard protocol.

Asymmetric encryption : HPKE with (MLKEM768-X25519 a.k.a. X-Wing, HKDF-SHA256, AES-128-GCM), or age with PQ keys.

Website or client-server application security : If you’re in the cloud, use its ALB/NLB. Otherwise, rustls, Go’s crypto/tls, BoringSSL, AWS-LC, or s2n-tls with a popular, updated ACME client.

Online backups : restic with a long random password.

If you’re in the cloud, KMS . Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128 .

Ptacek, 2015 : NaCl/libsodium default, or ChaCha20Poly1305, or AES-GCM.

Latacora, 2018 : KMS, or XSalsa20+Poly1305.

Latacora, 2024 : KMS, or NaCl’s secretbox, or XChaCha20Poly1305.

Latacora’s reasoning for why and when you’d use your cloud’s KMS is still solid, so start there.

If you’re encrypting locally, you want an AEAD where you can avoid worrying about tracking nonces or how many messages you encrypted, so you want random nonces of at least 128 bits. 2

NaCl/libsodium’s secretbox is just a paper-thin wrapper around a less common AE construction (XSalsa20+Poly1305), so instead I recommend XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305. The former is an efficient composition of a standard KDF and AES-GCM, packaged as an extended-nonce AEAD, so even if your library doesn’t provide it under that name you can assemble it from the KDF and AES-GCM APIs. 3

Regular AES-GCM and ChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces are only ok if you know for certain you won’t encrypt more than a billion messages with one key. AES-GCM-SIV is also a good AEAD choice if you happen to have it everywhere you need it, but that’s kinda unlikely. Some even newer options have nice properties like key commitment, but are not commonly available yet.

Since you have an AEAD, consider putting context in the additional data, like the user ID you’re encrypting for, or the version of the protocol. Anything not secret that you will definitely still know at decrypt time.

Very important is how you handle large messages, which KMS will not solve for you. Do not pass one large message to an AEAD, or you might be forced to process or store the plaintext before having authenticated it at decrypt time.…

An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
items.content:
No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we’ve seen usually happens away from workers—you’re taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you’re doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

In many ways, robotics and AI are well suited to the relentless pace of work that is already happening inside e-commerce fulfillment centers. Amazon’s promise of speedy deliveries for its 200 million Prime subscribers in particular requires hundreds of thousands of human employees to speedily assemble and ship out customer orders that often combine a dizzying array of products.

Much of the work in fulfillment centers also frequently involves “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks that people may prefer to hand over to robots. The injury and illness rate for workers in the US warehouse sector has typically been more than double the average across all industries, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration .

“You have almost 2 million people working in the warehousing sector in the United States, and it’s characterized by very high turnover and very high workplace injury rates,” said Greenwood.

But robots are still far from capable of handling the many different tasks that human workers can perform. So Amazon still has a massive human workforce working in tandem with the company’s growing fleet of wheeled robots and robotic arms—and workplaces can get complicated when humans are expected to keep pace with robotic counterparts.

Amazon has rapidly built its robotic fleet following the pivotal decision to acquire the robotics company Kiva Systems in 2012. Kiva was among the earliest companies to pioneer wheeled mobile robots that bring racks of items to warehouse workers, instead of requiring people to continually walk around grabbing items off of shelves inside fulfillment centers.

Since the acquisition, Kiva was renamed Amazon Robotics and has focused on deploying an array of mobile robots and robotic arms that Amazon primarily manufactures in-house at facilities in Massachusetts. This year, the company also announced it would build additional production factories in Austin, Texas, and Greenwood, Indiana , to churn out even more robots in the future.

“There’s a theme of how we look at the challenges that we can help our associates and our employees with, and how we can make our customers’ lives better through these technologies,” Scott Dresser , vice president of Amazon Robotics, told Ars. “Each step of the way, [we are] tackling a hard or deep set of technical challenges to achieve that goal.”

items.title: The baffling intelligence of a single cell (2024)
items.content:
I want to tell the story of a beautiful phenomenon in biology. In some

sense it’s the prototype of much of the activity of life. The

phenomenon is the way in which an individual cell of

E. coli forages for nutrients. This process, known as

“chemotaxis”—the “chemo-” for chemical and the “taxis” from the Greek

τάξις, for tactics—is intelligence in one of

its most elemental forms. An individual E. coli has no brain,

obviously, and is even many orders of magnitude simpler than a human

cell, and yet already it possesses something like a sense of smell,

drive, even a memory. Chemotaxis recasts E. coli not as some

aimless gut-pest but rather as an exquisitely sophisticated

I never liked the way biology was taught in high school . It was too much about the names of things. A subject so vast is

spoiled by a textbook, which can only point at the endless parade of

stuff-there-is-to-know. It’s better approached with questions—like

“what’s happening when you smell?” or ”what is a fever,

actually?”—that contemplate narrow, deep slices.

Chemotaxis is a great slice: it’s a triumph of systems biology—we

understand it holistically but also in fine detail at almost every

level. It acquaints you with many of the most important motifs in

biology, including the way in which protein structure determines

function; how membranes control the information flow into cells; and

how chemical modifications store and communicate state. It involves

one of the most sophisticated and beautiful pieces of molecular

nanotechnology, the flagellar motor. And it helps give an intuition

for how a bag of unthinking chemicals could possibly give rise to a

random direction (a “tumble”). By running when the getting is good and

tumbling when it isn’t, the E. coli takes a meandering path

A little more detail now: there are half a dozen or so rotors on the

E. coli’s body, each controlling a long whip-like tail that

flows behind it. When all the rotors are spinning in the same

direction, the tails join together into a coil that torques the cell

forward into a run. When even one rotor is spinning against the

others, the coil unbundles and E. coli spins into a tumble.

In a uniform chemical environment, the E. coli swims in a

random walk by balancing runs with periodic tumbles. By default, a run

lasts about a second, or ten times longer than a tumble. The rate of

runs versus tumbles, and their relative duration, is carefully tuned

to balance “exploitation” and “exploration”: if runs happened too

often or lasted too long, E. coli would range too widely and

zip past its food; too seldom or too short, and it’d likely never find

But how is this balance achieved? The crux of it is a signaling

bouncing around in the cytoplasm of the E. coli , interacting

items.title: Speeding up the Unreal editor by… not using unnecessarily secure hash methods
items.summary: performance
items.content:
One good trick when trying to look for ways to optimize software is to stay away from areas that are very likely already quite well optimized, and instead focus on areas that might have been overlooked, either because they are too obscure or don’t show up during regular profiling sessions. This tactic worked well in the past, as shown with my optimization of tooltip creation , or the loading of editor localization files .

So when profiling the editor launch (again), this is why I mostly skip over any functions that contain words like “Shader Compilation” or “Shader Source” when I stumble over them in my profiler. The compilation of shaders is a famously long and elaborate process, and I’m pretty sure that very smart people at Epic already spent a lot of time optimizing those areas. That’s the reason why I would, for example, skip the function “Compile Global Shader Map,” even though its runtime would be typically multiple seconds:

This was, at least, true until one day I skipped over it using an unusually high zoom level and saw one of the functions that was called by it:

I am certainly not an expert for hash algorithms, but SHA1 is one of the (very few) hash algorithms that even I know. And seeing this hash algorithm being used to hash shaders seemed somehow wrong to me. That’s because SHA1 is was a cryptographically safe hashing algorithm, originally developed by the NSA (yes, that one). And even though it has been cryptographically  broken years ago and actually shouldn’t be used for sensitive information anymore, this origin means that it is – to put it politely – not particularly fast.

What does not fast mean in this context? Well see for yourself in this comparison test of a bunch of commonly used hash algorithms that Aras Pranckevičius did a few years ago (actually, it was 10 years ago – I’m getting old). SHA1 was not even included as an actual competitor, but as the start of the article notes just “to illustrate the performance differences.” Ouch.

That’s especially annoying since the data being hashed is the shader source code, including all comments and copyright notice:

This means both that we have to hash a lot of data (source files can be quite big) and that there is no reason to hash it using a cryptographically secure hash, since it is no sensitive data.

Therefore, not using a cryptographically safe but fast hash algorithm should be an easy win, right? And the linked article already presented a good alternative, for which I even found an existing implementation in Unreal’s code base: xxHash.

Note before somebody asks: xxHash is not necessarily the fastest hash. Other, potentially even faster hashes do exist, but for now, using a faster hash that is already a used and tested part of the engine we are working on is a much more straightforward option.

Changing the used hash wasn’t too complicated, even though I had to change more places in the code than expected, since all places where the produced hash was stored or passed also had to be updated. A nice side effect of this change was that the stored hashes were a bit smaller than before (8 instead of 20 bytes).

But, of course, the effect that I made the change for wasn’t about memory, but CPU time. For testing purposes, I opened one of Unreal’s own sample projects, Electric Dreams , in the editor 5 times, both with and without the change, for a total of 10 runs. Profiling was done with Superluminal .

To put the following numbers into perspective, let me note that I will mostly talk about the overall CPU time, summed up over all threads, not just the time on the game thread. This is not done to artificially inflate the numbers, but to make the numbers more consistent and easier to compare. The actual effect on the editor start time is (very roughly) the measured time divided by the number of cores.

Social media is busy with claims that something dramatic just happened to the online environment.

Huge numbers of posts claim that that Russian bot traffic has fallen dramatically across the internet. And, with that, so has the number of posts and replies from automated accounts on sites such as X, formerly Twitter, and Facebook , the posts claim.

It has led to something of a trend on X, in which users post what they call a “bot test”: an opinion or claim of the kind that would ordinarily lead to an influx of automated responses. Some users do indeed claim that they have seen a substantial reduction in the number of replies of a certain kind, and use that to suggest both that the previous responses were from automated accounts and that those accounts have reduced in number.

It follows attacks on data centres run by Yandex, the company often referred to as Russia’s Google . They are part of a broad effort by Ukraine to attack the country’s internet infrastructure .

It is true that, in the wake of the attack, traffic from automated systems has fallen. Data from internet infrastructure company Cloudflare shows a small reduction in “bot traffic” over recent days, for instance.

Smoke billows from Yandex's Sasovo hub from a fire following a drone strike ( Social media )

That is particularly pronounced for traffic from Yandex, which typically accounts for a large amount of automated traffic within Russia . Cloudflare’s data shows the effect of the attack dramatically: on Sunday morning, after the attack, it drops to nearly zero, and is yet to recover to normal levels.

That is in line with statements from Yandex, which says that it is working to restore access to its services. Some of them are still entirely offline, it said in a statement on Sunday.

But it does not necessarily suggest that bots of the kind that post on social media have reduced their activity, or that there has been any meaningful result in the amount of misinformation or general posts from such accounts. While some users have reported that they are seeing less of those posts and accounts, that is not necessarily broadly true and may have nothing to do with the attacks on Yandex.

That is because Cloudflare ’s “bot” data measures traffic from non-human, automated sources in general. And those kinds of bots can be used for all purposes, both good and bad.

That bad activity is well known, and various. As well as automated accounts being used on social media to quickly spread misinformation or other problematic posts, they can also be used to search the internet for personal information or launch more specific cyber attacks.

However, bots are used for plenty of good or morally neutral purposes, too. One of the key contributors to such bot traffic is “crawlers”, which scan the internet to gather up data.

That can be used to update search engines or to collect data that can be used to train artificial intelligence systems, for instance. Both of those activities are done by Yandex, in much the same way they are used by Google and other rivals.

As such, those widely shared charts do not in themselves suggest that there will be any less activity from automated systems that post on social media. And there is nothing necessarily to suggest that the attacks have had any impact in that way at all.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

I’m most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so:

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here’s an illustration lifted from the documentation :

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. items.title: The Making Of Super Mario 64 – full Giles Goddard interview (2001)
items.content:
Seeing as it’s Mario’s 25th birthday and all that, seems like a good time for this!

This is the unpublished, unedited version of a 2001 interview with Nintendo coder Giles Goddard about the making of the N64’s Super Mario 64. Parts of this appeared in NGC magazine (that article is referenced on the Super Mario 64 Wikipedia page ), but this much bigger version has lots of juicy behind-the-scenes ’90s-era Nintendo stuff that didn’t make it into the article.

The notes are a bit rough. And the ‘questions’ are all guesses as to what I originally asked – for some reason I didn’t keep a record of what I actually asked at the time. Fool!

I can’t remember what my official title was, but I think I was front-end programmer or something like that. I basically just did the Mario face. It was supposed to be something like it was loading – even though it wasn’t on CD there was still lots of stuff going on in the background, sorting itself out.

How many people were on the Super Mario 64 team?

Probably about 15 people in the end. Probably not as many as people think. But then again there was some other people doing stuff behind the scenes. Compared with Zelda [Ocarina Of Time] , it was a very small team.

It was an open-plan office, but everybody had their own little cubicle. Depending on what projects they’re working on, they shift around. It is all open plan, in as much as you have rows of people sitting there working. But then where’s there a project going on, the core team would basically grab hold of these programmers and artists around them, and you’d get the Super Mario group expanding outwards from the centre.

I think at that time the artists and the programmers were actually separated out, so you had an artist group and a programmer group. I was actually right behind the Mario programmers team who were working with SGI on the N64 APIs and stuff. That part was quite small, so you could stand up and shout at someone who was working on Wave Race just away from someone working on Mario 64. Quite a good little set-up.

No talking! Particularly in Japanese companies, it’s very very quiet. Occasionally you’d get little groups of programmers or artists getting together for a chat, and somebody higher up would walk over and give them the eye, and they’d sit down and shut up. It’s nothing like English or US companies.

What kickstarted the Super Mario 64 project?

Well, obviously it was the first game, another Mario game was the most obvious game to do. It started way before there was any hardware, it started on these Onyx emulators, the old SGI Onyx. They had an N64 emulator, the first thing we got from SGI. It was an emulation of the API, not the hardware. At that time, Nishida-san – main programmer who started the entire project off – he was working on a GL and this emulator.

The emulator was quite close to the GL, so he had these little Mario characters running around on the Onyx, or API Indys later.

There was only 3 or 4 projects going on at EAD by that time, he was in charge of all of them. Three of those weren’t high priority, so he was 100% Mario 64, he was always there. Sitting down with a machine and playing with the various demos. One of the things he loved doing was just playing down with experiments.

That’s the way the Mario face came about. At the time, I was thinking of things to make that would show off what N64 could do. One of the things was real-time vertex calculations. In games, you usually have a fixed set of vertices that you simply move around in a matrix – you just move a shape around. We wanted to move around individual points, morph it. No games used it at the time, we didn’t know what to call it, so I named it meshes or something like that. I was playing around with this thing with a GL program on the Indy, playing around with this Mario face with an Indy cam, a cam you get with Indy – two ping-pong balls for a face. Miyamoto said: can you make a Mario face out of that for the N64?

I was mapping the OAuth flow that Google’s developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Google’s sign-in page. No account needed:

'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F'

The cookie is what caught my eye. Flask’s usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> , but about 1,200 bytes, way more than you need for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it.

Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed:

The " b" key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and pickletools.dis printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields:

client_id = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com"

The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload, which was bad enough on its own. It also carried Google’s OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.)

I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs.

A client secret leaking in a cookie is a finding on its own. The part that mattered was that the same value verified the signature, so I nailed that down properly instead of trusting a lucky guess.

Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline:

derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b "cookie-session" , "sha1" )

I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take.

The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it:

That pickle.loads is only “safe” as long as nobody else can forge a valid cookie. Once the key is public, that assumption is worthless. I built my own session with a made-up CSRF token and put whatever pickle I wanted under the matching flow key:

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
items.content:
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.

A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.

If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Intel D270 GPU AI Accelerator–Up to 480 GB LPDDR5X
'AI' is Not a Tool
items.summary: vibecoding
items.content:
(I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more)

First order of business - is ' tool ' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"?

We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later).

a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function

an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work

What I like best - A tool is something you wield .

wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control

Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use

Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc

Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events

Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try").

Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc.

What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself.

As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools.

Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation .

automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control.

A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code.

You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback.

What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right incantations. You are only a software update from everything you've 'learned' being rendered obsolete by the latest algorithm. (A soggy cold burger from which the onions have been removed) You have traded working with the world to working for a capricious robot.

It is a mistake to be haphazard about "tools" being equivalent to utility, e.g. saying - "the LLM didn't write my paper, I just used it as a tool to read and summarize some research papers". But you didn't wield it to read those papers (as you might a Kindle). It read the papers, not you.

What do you miss by abdicating doing the reading? Pretty much everything. First and foremost, you miss learning how to write from those who can. You miss learning how to formulate an argument. You miss noticing things. You miss loading your background mind with fodder for novel ideas. You miss building trust in some authors and suspicion of others. You miss all the jokes. You miss all of the edges. You miss learning how to think.

items.title: French supermarkets suffer refrigerator shutdown after 'unprecedented' cyberattack
items.content:
Intermarche was one of the groups affected — Gabriel BOUYS / AFP

Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.

Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented".

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality".

At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.

Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.

BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores".

Those branches that were affected will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP.

Specialist French retail sector news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this.

E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores".

A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.

Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates".

It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware". It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected.

A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cyber security agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor".

"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread", the source added.

The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since Sunday night.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he wrote on X.

He added that the company's teams were "fully mobilised" to restore the situation as quickly as possible.

"An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack," he added.

The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires", the prosecutor's office said.

Intermarche condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures.

BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products".

The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks.
